Ask #2: Change the composition of the M.S. degree such that it straightforwardly requires the completion of 30 credits of MHM credits.
Currently, the M.S. degree is structured as the combination of (1) one 12-credit post-baccalaureate certificate, (2) a second post-bac certificate, (3) one MHM elective, and (4) a practicum capstone.
This totals 10 MHM classes and 30 MHM credits.
The certificate portion of this is a so-called stackable certificate approach, with 24 of the 30 credits coming from these two post-bac certificates.
Our desire is to streamline the M.S. in Healthcare Management degree such that it is comprised of 30 MHM credits whether or not a student completes a graduate certificate en passant.
Our primary objective with this entire change proposal is #1 above – to make earning a graduate certificate in healthcare management at URI more accessible.
Per URI Online recruiters and prospectors, there has not been a single expression of interest in the post- bac certificate in quality improvement.

Students are certainly interested in quality improvement and this is an important topic in healthcare; however, none have expressed a desire to devote an entire program of study to this subject.
Any interest in earning a healthcare grad certificate at URI has been directed toward the other existing certificate in health administration.
Additionally, prospective students have expressed strong interest in being able to earn a certificate by taking courses outside of the strict structure that currently exists (at present, three of the four courses in each certificate are prescribed).
The current structure limits when students can begin and complete a certificate – they must wait until the carousel of courses comes back around for them to hop on, and in some cases that can be a year-long wait.
Creating a single certificate in healthcare management enables URI to alleviate these pain points and reach a wider audience of prospective students.
We have found that most prospective students interested in a grad certificate wish to begin quickly, and URI Online has the structure in place to enable that to happen.
The limiting factor is our current program design.

A side effect of creating a single graduate certificate in healthcare management is that the “stackable certificate” design of the M.S. would need to go away and be replaced with a straightforward 30-credit MHM approach.
There is no evidence that removing the notion of stackable certificates would do harm.
No prospects in recent memory have expressed interest in earning the stackable certificates as a pathway to the M.S. degree.
In fact, it has created confusion during prospect calls and sessions. 2

As a final sidenote on the topic of stackable certificates, in my professional opinion (as a scholar of human resources) such a design may even adversely impact URI’s ability to provide accessible healthcare management graduate education to Rhode Islanders and beyond.

Some graduate certificate programs around the country do qualify for federal aid, but our healthcare management ones were determined not to.
Thus, students must pay for all certificate credits (up to 24 under the current “stackable” model) with non- federal financial aid, such as out of pocket or via private loans.
At current rates, that amounts to $18,792 for two URI certificates.
This has led to more than one prospective student not applying or enrolling at URI this summer and fall.
The streamlining we propose potentially removes barriers to access and may help put URI graduate education within reach for more aspiring healthcare professionals and leaders.

Summary: In sum, the newly-proposed M.S. degree structure would include all the same courses as before.
We are not changing the curricular offering at all - we are simply proposing that the stackable certificate design be removed.
That’s ask #2 above.
And we are asking for it to be removed because we wish to offer a single grad certificate in healthcare management that offers flexibility and frequency for learners (instead of two separate certificates that are narrowly tailored).
That’s ask #1 above. 6.

VP Preisser and Senators Meenach, Van Wyk, Trimm and Daniels were present. 2.
Minutes for approval - i.
Minutes of the 1/16/26 FSEC meeting - Approved as edited.
Ii.
Minutes of the 1/22/26 FS meeting - Tabled. 3.
Priority Items (40 minutes) 3.1 New ‘home’ for the Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Graduate Programs - The three INP graduate programs (MS, PhD and Certificate) were administratively re-homed from the Graduate School to CHS as a result of the December senate meeting.
Senate officers have heard inquiries and concerns about that move and it appears that a process improvement should be implemented that might ensure program directors are not left out of these decisions.

There were questions about the origins of such proposals and why the system is built in such a way that deans can leapfrog relevant faculty.
Beyond the mechanics of Kuali proposals, there seems to be a need to develop a better model for how interdisciplinary programs are housed at the university.
Pres.
Williams will try to learn more about the genesis of this particular change and the approval process it was subjected to.
FSEC may circle back with tangible suggestions for process improvements but in the meantime, staff was asked to pay particular attention to “administrative” requests in Kuali and alert the FSEC or senate officers to any concerns.
Sen.
Trimm will communicate with CASC about how to approach such proposals, if necessary, and VP Preisser will do the same with the Graduate Council. 3.2 Future Legislation Updates i.
Establishing College Liaisons - The FSEC Officers are meeting with the Council of Deans next week (2/4) and hope to gather their input and use it to refine the draft. ii.
College By-Laws - This remains a secondary priority behind the Liaisons.
FSEC members agree that once the liaison roles are established and liaisons start meeting together, 1

shared information about the disparate operations of the colleges will help make a case for a By-laws mandate or other common governance structure requirements. iii.
Chapter 8 amendments related to 7 & 14 week calendar alignment - VP Preisser provided a synopsis of the plan to roll out a four program pilot of concurrent enrollment options in Fall, 2027.
The affected colleges will need to vote in favor of the plan in order for it to go forward.
The pilot will be subject to review and renewal at the end of four years.
If the Senate elects to reject renewal, the concurrent enrollments will end at the conclusion of the spring, 2031 term.
If the senate determines that the system is working well, the initiative could be expanded.
Questions were asked about the basis for renewal and if expectations can and will be set for a meaningful evaluation.
There was also a concern about institutional memory given that senators sitting at roll-out will cycle off the senate prior to the renewal phase.
VP Preisser noted that it will be up to the programs themselves to initiate their renewal so the senate will not need to ‘remember’ to do it.

A final draft is expected today and FSEC agreed to forward it to TAAC, CBUM and the ACC for review.
The legislation will be introduced in February and docketed for action in March, if ready. iv.
Clarifying and specifying launch date for SGO and 4+ attempt legislation - Staff is preparing amendments to FSEC Bills 4 and 5 to include the effective dates (Fall 2026) and will ensure that future bills all include an effective date. v.
Approval of academic calendars 8 years in advance - The Graduate School has expressed a need to set the calendar eight years in advance and such a change would require amending Sec. 8.70.10 of the UM, which prescribes a 6-year calendar.
This move would temporarily add to the workload of the ACC, which would be tasked with preparing and presenting for approval two additional calendars all in one year.
The Committee is responsible for setting the Summer, Online, standard academic year calendars, including J-term, but would need to close the gap between the 6- and 8- years out versions.
The amendment itself is straightforward and could be introduced in February. vi.

Adjusting due date for final grades - There are concerns about the timelines associated with faculty entering final grades after exams, academic standing notifications being generated, and students having adequate time to react to those notifications, especially if they need to file a grade appeal or are facing a negative finding regarding their academic standing.
URI faculty often benefit from ample time to report grades, but sometimes face quicker turnarounds.
The administration recently suggested running an AI model to determine a standard that might be optimal for students,faculty, and advising staff.
FSEC members suggested that no such effort is likely necessary, because a quick look at the due dates for the last four years reveals that faculty have not faced a deadline earlier than six days post-exam.
It would be simple and probably agreeable to simply establish that time frame as a standard.
There was some concern about the fall semester in particular, since the deadline could bump up against the Christmas holiday.
Pres.

Williams revealed that Fannon Institute Director Kim Stack has done some research on this matter and found that at most peer institutions, the norm for grade posting is 72 hours after the exam is completed.
It will be important to emphasize that the time of the staff involved in generating the standing reports is valuable too, and a balance needs to be struck between faculty preferences and the needs of staff to generate adequate and timely reports that serve students’ needs. 2

3.3 Missing Classroom Database (circling back) - Pres.
Williams reported that he has communicated with the JCSC and the CTI about the initiative to restore the database as a resource.
It is hoped that they will make substantial progress before the end of the academic year. 3.4 Campus restrooms/Washrooms/Religious observances (circling back) - Pres.
Williams noted the database of single user facilities has been updated as a web resource but it does not provide any intersection with accessible facilities.
This still needs to happen.
It was also recently noted that washroom needs related to cultural and religious practices should likely be addressed but this would be an extensive project with multiple stakeholders.
It does not appear the senate has the bandwidth to tackle it this year so VP Preisser was encouraged to keep it on his radar for next year. 3.5 Advance Planning - 2/19/26 FS meeting - The agenda was reviewed and a suggestion was made about adding the 7 & 14 week calendar alignment language.

FSEC still has another week before it needs to approve the agenda for posting. 3.6 Advance Planning - AY 26-27 FS meeting schedule - It was noted recently that this year’s confluence of an FSEC meeting, the first day of classes and a senate meeting proved to be a lot for many faculty.
Staff offered a calendar draft for next year so that FSEC has the opportunity to weigh all options before presenting something to the senate.
The current draft attempts to standardize the third Thursday each month, consistent with the Manual, and takes into account all religious holidays when work is not permitted. 3.7 Senate role in approving a new institute (CHILD Institute) - The CIRC has approved the creation of a new Institute.
Committee Liaison Meenach will ask the Chair of CIRC to prepare a brief report for the next Senate meeting and attach all supporting documents so the senate might review it as required. 3.8 MPS rehoming (circling back) - Pres.
Williams reached out to the departments involved in the Program to gain feedback on the re-homing to the College of Education from the Graduate School.
There seemed to be some misunderstanding of how the budget model works.

It requires that the “money follows the instructor” which means that the departments will keep revenue for their courses and those funds will not be diverted to the CoEdu.
But there does seem to be opacity around the administrative apparatus.
The college is simply responsible for ‘stacking’ the certificates that the departments offer, and will likely get to count the graduates in their degree conferral numbers.
It remains unclear how those numbers factor in as KPIs under the budget model, so the move could still have a budgetary impact even though the direct course revenue path is well-defined.
FSEC will need to monitor in an ongoing way and be mindful of any other administrative changes that are proposed, as they could have similar unpredictable consequences. 4.
Continued Items 4.1 Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - No new concerns. 5.
Updates 5.1 Updates (meetings with administrators, other committee meetings) i.
APC review - Textbook and course materials policy - reviewers requested - Pres.
Williams explained that the use of the campus bookstore as a comprehensive course materials outlet is absolutely essential.

It does not have to be the only avenue available to students but does need to be an option.
Although there have been well-known delays and complications in the bookstore securing 3

materials, the alternatives pursued by faculty in lieu of the bookstore can easily become a logistical and ethical minefield.
Concerns were expressed that the current bookstore retailer has attempted to force faculty to standardize course materials across all sections of a given course and this is a serious infringement of faculty rights.
The FS Pres. and VP met earlier with the Student Senate President who voiced a concern that textbook affordability has become a serious issue for undergraduates.
Federal mandates around student aid use make bookstore cooperation even more important.
That being said, the APC is about to update its Textbook and Course Materials Policy and has asked the FSEC officers and other volunteers to serve as reviewers; Sens.
Daniels and Trimm volunteered.
Policy readers are asked to review the draft carefully and provide margin notes or other comments and concerns for APC staff. ii.
PSC meeting of 1/27/26 - The meeting included a report about the university's transition away from Ecampus HR to WorkDay (the State as a whole has already transitioned).

If all goes well, the university may consider transitioning to WorkDay’s student module in the future. iii. ‘Survey Design Advising Team’ - JVW Sen.
Van Wyk consented to launch and manage this service for the foreseeable future.
Pres.
Williams noted he needs to present the idea to the Provost’s office for a reaction before the initiative goes to the senate, possibly for a March introduction.
The senate office is happy to host the resource and forms on their webpage with links to the Provost’s pages, if desired. iv.
Senate appointments to Library Dean search - Pres.
Williams has completed the appointment of two faculty members. v.
Copyright statement - No report ; still under review by the General Counsel. vi.
Commencement schedule - FSEC assignments - TBD following election of a new VP/President-elect (on 2/29), who should be given the opportunity to choose the extent of their role. vii.
Chapter 2 UM amendments - Status of revisions - for February adoption?
There were some related concerns about the decision to split the position of the Vice Provost for Academic Personnel and Budget in two.

Some edits to the draft are in progress and it is hoped that the senate is still on track to accept the changes in February. 6.
Report of the Coordinator i.
Student worker hiring update - The FS office is on-boarding two graduate student workers who are starting right away. ii.
Senate elections and February VP election - Staff is waiting for the current full-time faculty list from the Provost’s team which is required to prepare apportionment notices.
The office is also designing an electronic ballot for the VP election, which will run differently this year than in years past due to new UM updates. iii.
Parliamentarian - The FS Parliamentarian serves at the pleasure of the FS President and this individual does not need to be a senator to serve.
If the current Parliamentarian continues past his term expiration, FSEC should consider providing compensation.
FSEC members agreed unanimously. iv.
New question - What prevents a faculty member from teaching in another department?
This question was raised to staff from a sitting senator who offered the example of an Engineering faculty member being qualified to teach calculus or physics from inside the engineering department.

FSEC members explained that course codes belong to department heads;additionally, per the AAUP contract, chairs are responsible for assigning teaching responsibilities. 7.
New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda. 4

i. Changes to qualifications for emeritus status - Some concerns have been transmitted to the Provost’s office and FSEC is waiting for a reply. ii. Brightspace purge - Faculty are complaining about the loss of resources but FSEC members agreed the 5-year horizon is more than reasonable and faculty members have the option of archiving materials themselves. It is not expected that the university will have Brightspace ‘forever’ and FSEC members queried if there is a plan in place for archiving or recovering materials after Brightspace is offboarded. Pres. Williams will assign the CTI the task of gleaning more information. iii. multiple paid resources for communications (CTI issue) - Tabled to next week’s meeting. 8. Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting. A question was asked about the recent Snow Day, wherein faculty were prevented from offering any remote synchronous options. Pres. Williams noted that decision was the result of the university’s Weather and Other Emergencies Policy wherein that stipulation is clear. Asynchronous options are not affected. 9. Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 2:34 pm. 5

Summary description of proposed program (not to exceed 2 pages) The information age has brought advancements in technology and data collection techniques that produce an abundance of accessible data in all sectors and created a new paradigm for science, based on data-intensive computing.
The ever-increasing data is often unstructured and requires development of new techniques for storage, analysis, and effective decision making.
Data science is the study of complex data or big data.
It involves developing methods to collect, record, store, analyze, and interpret data to effectively extract useful information and detect patterns, trends, and relationships in data sets for decision-making purposes.
The data scientist is often a storyteller presenting data insights to decision makers in a way that is understandable and applicable to their interests.

2 The field of data science, including data mining and machine learning, is interdisciplinary at its core, drawing upon skills in computer science, mathematics, statistics, and ethics.
Its primary goal is to gain insights and knowledge from any type of data, both structured and unstructured, and provide important resources to organizations that make data-driven decisions.
As new technologies are developed, data science will continue to grow in importance to business, industry, science, many academic disciplines, healthcare, and government in the years ahead.
Data scientists are employed in many settings, including finance & insurance, professional services, healthcare & social assistance, retail trade, and manufacturing.
Top industries hiring data scientists: Information Technology & Services, Computer Software, Internet, Financial Services, and Higher Education.
Although Hanover’s Market Opportunity Scan: National Degree Programs (Updated), prepared for URI in July 2018, does not explicitly address programs in data science, it does address the potential for a graduate certificate in Artificial Intelligence, which is closely related to machine learning, a core subject of data science.

The market analysis suggests using the development of such a graduate certificate as "a vehicle for career advancement that requires less time and resources than a master’s degree.” Furthermore, the analysis suggests that "the labor market demand for artificial intelligence professionals is strong, and that related fields (including computer and information research science and software development) are projected to add 121,000 jobs per year between 2016 and 2026.” Indeed, not many online certificate programs in artificial intelligence exist today outside of one at Johns Hopkins and one at Stanford.
Regarding data science, Lewis University has an online Graduate Certificate in Data Science and Cornell has an online Graduate Certificate in Data Analytics, which has a business focus.
Today, the job prospects for Data Scientists are strong.
Currently, of the approximately 134,000 open job announcements for data science or data scientist listed on Indeed.com, approximately 1,700 are entry level positions.

Since its inception five years ago, Glassdoor ranked Data Scientist as one of the top 10 best jobs in America, based on median base salary, the number of active job openings, and employee satisfaction rates, with a #1 ranking in 2016, 2017, and 2018.
LinkedIn’s 2020 Emerging Jobs Report ranks Data Scientist as #3 in the list of Top 15 Emerging Jobs in the U.S.
The report states, “It’s a specialty that’s continuing to grow significantly across all industries.
Our data indicates some of this growth can likely be attributed to the evolution of previously existing jobs, like statisticians, and increased emphasis on data in academic research.” Robert Half Technology, a search firm, produced the Salary Guide 2020, in which they list salaries for Data Scientists between $105K and $180K, depending on the geographical location, experience, and expertise of the employee.
They state that “upskilling” is a priority for most IT departments as they grow skill sets in-house.
After conducting a survey, they found that 90% of technology managers are upskilling some of their employees.
Data science and machine learning are among the most common areas for professional development.

Companies upskilling in-house employees represent a potential market for this program, as they may fund their employees to enroll in this program as part of their professional development.
The time is right.
With the growth in jobs, will come learner demand and URI will have one of the first Online graduate certificate programs in data science offered by an accredited university.
This certificate, as is suggested in the Hanover report, will be marketed as a “vehicle for career advancement that requires less time and resources than a master’s degree.” There are many reasons why someone might seek a certificate in data science.
One may be looking to switch to a more lucrative career or improve their skills to achieve a higher level within their profession.
With job prospects decreasing in some areas, adding data science skills could greatly enhance career opportunities.
One may even wish to pursue a master’s degree but get started with a certificate that is more quickly obtainable.

This program targets professionals seeking recent data analysis methods and technologies that could be applied into their current work roles; recent graduates (including those from URI) that are looking to expand their skills and land into data science related jobs; recent graduates who are interested in graduate programs in data science and related fields; students interested in data visualization to develop and communicate insights about the data; professionals who need data science skills to contribute to other fields; and current students in graduate programs seeking skills in data science to apply to their discipline.
